CMPS 3160 - Milestone 1 - Nora and Kyle¶

Predicting Equity Returns Using Macroeconomic and Fundamental Indicators Across Multiple Financial Databases¶

Mounted at /content/drive

Abstract:¶

This project will investigate equity return predictions using several sources of financial data. Three sources we are using include company fundamentals from Yahoo Finance, technical indicators from Wharton Research Data Services (LSEG), and macroeconomic data from the Federal Reserve Economic Data.

Combining these sources into one dataset, we hope to investigate which indicator may be the most predictive, which variables hurt equity performance, and if the combination of disparate sources can contribute to a more informed investment strategy.

Collaboration plan:¶

We have a shared Google Drive folder containing our Notebook, data sets, and Doc to draft ideas and make a to-do list. We communicate via email and determine which parts of each milestone we're each responsible for. We check in throughout the working process, and ask for feedback and help as needed.

Data Description:¶

The first data set we will be investigating is from the St. Louis Federal Reserve Bank. This data set contains four attributes;

Federal Funds Rate: The rate depository institutions (mainly banks) lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight, set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).

Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation: measures the average change over time in prices paid by urban consumers for a representative "basket" of goods and services. It is a key economic indicator used to gauge the purchasing power of currency and cost-of-living changes.

10-year minus 2-year treasury yield spread: Compares the return rates of long and short term investments, such as bonds. Can serve as an indicator for consumer confidence and serve as a barometer for the economy.

Unemployment rate: The percentage of the laborforce that doesn't have a job.

Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/

Data pulled using an API key

This data set has one observation for the first of each month from 2005 to 2025.

Although this data set does not contain our target variable of equity return, it can help represent and quantify critical, but more abstract, factors such as consumer confidence.

ETL¶

One interesting statistic that will be useful when other data is present is the average Federal Funds Rate. The Federal Funds Rate is an important metric for monetary policy in the U.S. and helps represents the cost of borrowing. This rate has an important function within financial markets since it affects different inputs in equity valuation models, which are models predicting what a company is or projected to be worth.

Lets calculate the average FFR from 2005 to 2025.

In [12]:
print("Average FFR: ", fred['Fed_Funds_Rate'].mean())

Average FFR:  1.697136929460581

Analyizing the data similarly but with varying date ranges can give interesting results. From 2009 to 2021, the FFR is close to zero, mainly as a result of the financial crisis in 2009 leading up to coronavirus. Now, the FFR has been averaging near 5 percent, which is pretty tight and increases the cost of borrowing. This also lowers the projected value of earnings and more negative pressure gets put on companies stock prices.

Another interesting statistic can be found in the yield spread, which is the difference between long term and short term treasury yields. Yield spreads are important for investing because it is a metric used when people are estimating a country’s economic growth, as well as their corporate earnings.

In [13]:
print("Average Yield spread: ", fred['Yield_Spread'].mean())

Average Yield spread:  0.9943983402489627

Accross the entire date range, the average is approximately 1.0. However we also see periods where the average yield spread is negative, such as a long stretch from 2022 - 2024. When yield spreads are negative, it can be an indicator that an economy is slowing or that recession is near, which is extremely important to know when investing in certain companies that are recession proof or volatile to recession.

A third intriguing statistic lies within the Consumer Price Index, which measures inflation. Inflation affects equity markets and investments a lot because it changes the expenses within corporations, and also is a major influencer of monetary policy. An important timeframe within this data was the movements between 2020 and 2023, where the index rose from 258 to 305. This captures the inflation increase post pandemic from several economic problems such as supply chains and or energy prices. This shows how much an economy is based on current events. Another reason inflation is a relevant metric is because of its effect on interest rates. When inflation is higher, interest rates tend to become higher causing lower stock valuations. It is important to take this into account when investing in certain economic times.

The graphic below shows the relationship between CPI and the Federal Funds Rate. It shows how when inflation increases, interest rates often rise. Note the scalar multiplier applied to the FFR to make the changes more apparant on the current y-scale.

Now, we will work on merging this data frame with our FRED data. LSEG pulls the annual reports that companies release, so we have one entry per year for each company. We will extend this data by copying the rows so it will match our format of the first of every month.

In [19]:
# Convert 'year_' to datetime objects representing the start of the year
lseg['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(lseg['year_'].astype(int), format='%Y')

# Create a list to store expanded rows
expanded_rows = []

# Iterate over each row in the lseg dataframe
for index, row in lseg.iterrows():
    base_date = row['Date']
    # Generate 12 months for each year
    for month_offset in range(12):
        new_date = base_date + pd.DateOffset(months=month_offset)
        new_row = row.copy()
        new_row['Date'] = new_date
        expanded_rows.append(new_row)

# Create the new expanded dataframe
lseg_expanded = pd.DataFrame(expanded_rows)

# Drop the original 'year_' column as it's replaced by 'Date'
lseg_expanded = lseg_expanded.drop(columns=['year_'])

#Put new data column back at the front of the dataframe
lseg_expanded.insert(1, 'Date', lseg_expanded.pop('Date'))

# Display the head of the expanded DataFrame to verify
display(lseg_expanded.head())

The last non-numerical data remaining is 'Ticker'. This is the name of the individual stock. It doesn't serve as a good index due to non-uinqueness, but also isn't useful for regression because it's categorical. We will drop it when doing regression, but for now, we will use it to create a more visually simple representation of our data in a Pivot table. The data is now grouped by stock, and each row is a date entry for that stock.

In [22]:
# Get all numerical columns except 'Ticker' and 'Date' for values
numerical_cols = lseg_fred.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()
pivot_values = [col for col in numerical_cols if col not in ['Date']]

# Create the pivot table
pivot_df = pd.pivot_table(lseg_fred, values=pivot_values, index=['Ticker', 'Date'], aggfunc=np.mean)

# Sort the pivot table by Ticker and then by Date
pivot_df = pivot_df.sort_values(by=['Ticker', 'Date'])

# Display the first few rows of the pivot table
display(pivot_df)

plt.show()

To make the date information more prominent, let's filter the pivot_df_scaled to focus on a single ticker, for example, 'AAPL'. This will allow us to see how the various indicators change over time for that specific company.

In [26]:
# Select a single ticker to visualize (e.g., 'AAPL')
single_ticker = 'AAPL'
filtered_df_scaled = pivot_df_scaled.loc[single_ticker]

# Ensure the Date is part of the index for plotting
# For multi-index, if you loc a specific ticker, Date becomes the new index.
# We might want to reset index for clear x-axis labels if preferred, but heatmap usually takes index as y-axis.
# For a single ticker, the index is now 'Date'.

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8))
sns.heatmap(filtered_df_scaled, cmap='viridis', yticklabels=filtered_df_scaled.index.strftime('%Y-%m'))
plt.title(f'Scaled Macroeconomic and Fundamental Indicators Heatmap for {single_ticker} Over Time')
plt.xlabel('Indicators')
plt.ylabel('Date')
plt.show()

This heatmap now clearly shows the evolution of each indicator for 'AAPL' over time, with the dates explicitly labeled on the y-axis. If you want to see overall trends across all companies, we would need to aggregate the data by date first (e.g., by taking the mean of all tickers for each month/year).

Let's now create a heatmap that aggregates the data by year across all tickers to observe overall yearly trends.

In [27]:
# Reset the index to access 'Date' as a column
aggregated_df = pivot_df_scaled.reset_index()

# Extract the year from the 'Date' column
aggregated_df['Year'] = aggregated_df['Date'].dt.year

# Group by year and calculate the mean for all numerical columns
# Exclude 'Ticker' as it's a categorical identifier and not relevant for numerical aggregation
yearly_avg_df = aggregated_df.groupby('Year')[numerical_cols].mean()

# Plot the heatmap of the yearly aggregated data
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 10))
sns.heatmap(yearly_avg_df, cmap='viridis')
plt.title('Yearly Aggregated Macroeconomic and Fundamental Indicators Heatmap (All Tickers)')
plt.xlabel('Indicators')
plt.ylabel('Year')
plt.show()

We can now begin preprocessing our data. Looking ahead, we're going to use Random Forest Regressor. This algorithm doesn't do well with Nan values, so we will first drop any rows where our target variable (ReturnOnEquityToTotal) isn't present. The loss of data will be minimal, and we choose over 40 companies to counteract this necessary loss.

Perfect! We can now begin building the primary steps for our model. The goal is to build a superscore metric out of our many available features to predict future preformance of individual stocks. First, we will analyze which features are the most impactful to the successful prediction.

In [30]:
# Train test split
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

x = lseg_fred.drop(columns=[target, 'Ticker', 'Date'])
y = lseg_fred[target]

x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
In [31]:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

# Initialize the Random Forest Regressor
rf_model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)

# Train the model
rf_model.fit(x_train, y_train)

We can see that total debt (to equity) seems to be one of the most important indicators for predicting equity performance. We will use this to inform our choices of data when building our final model.

Next steps¶

Next, we are working on accessing the other two data sets. Then, we need to decide how to best handle and incorperate the date data type into our overall dataset.
